summary: Software World Model (SWM) fine-tunes small Qwen2.5-Coder models (0.5B forecaster, 3B agent) with GRPO on executed counterfactual changes so that, before landing a change, a coding agent predicts which downstream consumers in other services or packages will break (the 'blast set'). On procedurally generated 4-7-service systems and two Python real-library worlds it beats the untrained base agent and the authors' 3B re-implementations of CWM and Qwen-AgentWorld on migration return, and beats typed dependency-graph reachability on failures through couplings the graph misses. The appendix concedes that a tabular logistic-regression risk scorer beats it on forecast F1, ranking regret and plan return, and that simply checking every consumer beats it at the paper's own prices.

claims.claim: Blast-set F1 improves from 0.431 (typed reachability) to 0.571 +/- 0.037 on held-out synthetic systems
claims.evidence: Table 8: preregistered shared-clip arm 0.565/0.537/0.611 over three seeds on 90 held-out forecast steps with a 0.5B model (Table 13); per-module clip gives 0.607. App B.3: 'Relation/action logistic regression has the highest aggregate F1 in this companion study', and reachability is better on direct propagation (App C.1). The number is real; the abstract omits the stronger simple baseline.

claims.claim: SWM more than halves candidate-ranking regret
claims.evidence: Table 3: regret 0.593 vs reachability 1.430 (-59%). App C.2: supervised controls reach regret 0.165-0.258, and even a noise-perturbed oracle at F1 0.213 has regret 1.343, so 'halves' is measured against the weakest comparator.

claims.claim: SWM improves migration return at all nine evaluation checkpoints
claims.evidence: Text gives only a pooled belief-plan return of 0.757 vs 0.685 for reachability (N=64, three-seed SE, 40 tasks); no per-checkpoint returns are tabulated. Section 4.4 states a supervised risk scorer has higher belief-plan return, and App C.3 shows checking every consumer reaches 0.826.

claims.claim: Training on executed consequences improves the same coding agent (synthetic return 0.721 -> 0.773; real libraries 0.453 -> 0.613), beating CWM and Qwen-AgentWorld
claims.evidence: Tables 1, 2, 4, 5: paired world-cluster bootstrap 95% intervals exclude zero for all four 360-record corpora (40 tasks, 7 held-out worlds); all 12 seeds improve. Real-library comparison has SDs but no intervals. Baselines are the authors' 3B re-implementations of 32B/35B+ originals. Random exploration (0.772) does as well as decision-aware (0.765) at 360 records, and the authors note no ordinary fine-tuning control.

claims.claim: On held-out real libraries, predicting structured failure outcomes rather than only scalar risk is important for downstream decision quality
claims.evidence: No section isolates structured vs scalar outputs. The scalar supervised risk scorer beats SWM on in-distribution F1 and plan return (Section 4.4) and on regret (App C.2), and the GRPO reward weights for outcome class and channel are 0.0 (Table 13).

patterns.note: Typed dependency graph (System-Surface Graph) reachability vs learned predictor on the same held-out forecasts (Fig 8b, App C.1): reachability has higher F1 on direct channels; the learned model wins on hidden channels (synthetic 0.304 vs 0.189; real libraries 0.198 vs 0.137). The 34.8% hidden-channel share is set by the authors' per-relation edge-drop rates (App D.4).

Cross-repo consumer protection: the learned predictor raises migration return over the untrained base agent (intervals exclude zero, 7 worlds), but checking every downstream consumer gives 0.826 vs 0.757 for the learned belief plan on the same 40 tasks (App C.3); the authors concede this in App D.9.

Execution beats prediction when checks are cheap: 'check every consumer' (0.826 at 0.01/check, 0.780 at 0.02) and 'always canary' (0.823) beat the learned belief plan (0.757) on the same 40 held-out tasks under the paper's own cost model (App C.3, D.9).

GRPO on executed outcomes beats the untrained base and 3B re-implementations of CWM/Qwen-AgentWorld, but a relation/action logistic regression beats it on forecast F1 and regret, and there is no ordinary fine-tuning control (Section 4.3).

Predicting a change's downstream blast set across repos is a pre-change discovery step, but the paper does not study discovery before writing a spec or plan; no comparison with human or tool-based discovery.

methodology.sample: Synthetic agent study: 40 migration tasks from 7 held-out procedurally generated worlds x 25 arms (1,000 episodes); forecasting: 90 held-out forecast steps; ranking: 90 choice sets / 340 candidates; planning: 40 tasks. Real libraries: marshmallow + 4 dependents and OpenTelemetry semantic conventions + 4 instrumentation packages; 984 held-out records with 137 graph-missed breaks. Acme (4 repos) and Online Boutique (10 repos) used for exploration.
methodology.baselines: Untrained base agent; authors' 3B re-implementations of CWM and Qwen-AgentWorld; typed reachability; action-only and relation/action logistic regression; GNN-only; zero-shot code models; empty/true-graph/oracle bounds. The logistic-regression control and check-every-consumer beat SWM but are absent from Table 1 and the abstract.
methodology.models: Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct 3B (agent), 0.5B (companion forecaster), 1.5B alternative; LoRA + supervised warmup + GRPO / SC-GRPO.
methodology.variance: Three training seeds; world-cluster bootstrap 95% intervals (10,000 resamples, 7 clusters) for synthetic agent ablations; SDs in Table 5; no intervals for the real-library agent comparison; three-seed half-ranges for forecasts.
methodology.ablations: Exploration policy x budget (100/200/360 records); nested graph-input richness and input budget (30 vs 60 edges); per-module vs shared gradient clipping; graph tokens; calibration; paid-check strategies.
methodology.contamination_controls: Training and evaluation worlds disjoint; real-library evaluation on libraries disjoint from training worlds; labels come from executed or deterministic propagation, not LLM judgments.
methodology.languages: Python (Flask services, marshmallow, OpenTelemetry); Online Boutique mixes Go, Node and Python; no Java.

standards.artifacts: No public code or data URL; the paper cites internal repository revisions and evidence files only
standards.preregistration: One recipe is labelled 'preregistered' (Table 8, App D.7) but no registry link is given

biases.detail: Headline comparisons are against an untrained base, the authors' own 3B re-implementations of CWM/Qwen-AgentWorld, and binary reachability; the strongest simple control (relation/action logistic regression) and check-every-consumer both beat SWM but are kept out of Table 1 and the abstract.
Synthetic systems have 4-7 services, 3 exported symbols and 2-column datastores; hidden-channel rates come from author-chosen drop probabilities (App D.4).
40 agent tasks from 7 held-out worlds; 90 forecast steps; two upstream real libraries.
Return uses author-chosen prices (0.25 per broken service, 0.05 per migration, 0.01-0.02 per check); whether prediction beats checking depends on these prices (App D.9).
Authors' own synthetic worlds, return metric and re-implemented baselines.
No code, worlds or trained checkpoints released.

coi.affiliations: Emory University; CausalDynamics.com (four authors, including the corresponding author as dual affiliate)
coi.detail: Company co-affiliation, but no commercial product is evaluated or promoted.

verdict_reason: Seeds, clustered bootstrap intervals, broad ablations and an unusually candid appendix. But the abstract's 'more than halves regret' and 'structured outcomes matter' are framed against the weakest comparators while a logistic-regression scorer and check-every-consumer beat SWM, the worlds are small and synthetic, and nothing is released. The most useful finding is the appendix's: graph reachability is better on recorded dependencies, learned or executed evidence is needed for couplings the graph misses, and cheap checks beat prediction.
applicability: For the team's several repositories this is about knowing what a change breaks downstream, which is part of discovery before writing a cross-repo spec. Three points transfer. First, a statically extracted dependency graph misses couplings through configuration, event topics and shared database columns, so a discovery step built only on a code graph should also enumerate consumers through Spring property keys, queue or topic names and shared tables. Second, when a downstream check is cheap (consumer contract tests, downstream test suites), running it beats any learned prediction, by the paper's own numbers. Third, the method itself needs resettable executable worlds plus GRPO training, which the team will not build. There is no Java evidence; it covers Python, Go and Node only.
